title: Tennessee Seller Disclosure: Condition Form and 1978 Rule
description: A plain-English look at the Tennessee seller disclosure: the residential property condition disclosure, the lead-based paint rule for pre-1978 homes, and next steps.
body:
If you are getting ready to list a home in Middle Tennessee, paperwork comes up before the first showing. Two items matter most for a Tennessee seller disclosure: the residential property condition disclosure, and for older homes, the lead-based paint disclosure.

This post explains how they work in plain terms. I am not an attorney, and this is not legal advice. Forms and rules can change, so check the Tennessee Real Estate Commission for current versions.

## Two disclosures with two different triggers

{{img:0}}

Tennessee sellers complete the residential property condition disclosure, or an exemption. The lead-based paint disclosure applies to homes built before 1978.

The two are triggered differently:

- The property condition disclosure is either completed or covered by an exemption.
- The lead-based paint disclosure depends on the year the home was built.

A home built before 1978 may involve both. A home built in 1978 or later falls outside the lead-based paint rule, but the condition disclosure question still applies.

## The residential property condition disclosure

This form gives buyers a written account of the home's condition from the person who has owned it. As a seller, you answer based on what you actually know.

A few habits make it easier:

- **Gather records first.** Repair invoices, warranty papers and past inspection reports help you answer accurately.
- **Answer from your own knowledge.** If you do not know something, say so instead of guessing.
- **Be complete.** If you know about a problem, the disclosure is the place to say so. It is better than waiting for an inspector to find it.
- **Do not assume an exemption.** Whether one applies to your sale is a question for your agent and the Tennessee Real Estate Commission, and for legal questions, an attorney you choose.

The goal is a true picture of the home. A form that is filled out carefully and honestly is easier for everyone to work from once a buyer is under contract.

## The 1978 lead-based paint rule

{{img:1}}

The lead-based paint disclosure applies to homes built before 1978. So the first step is confirming the year your home was built.

Your closing paperwork from when you bought is one place to look. County records are another. For a Williamson County address, the [Williamson County property search](https://www.williamsoncounty-tn.gov/2099/35739/Property-Data-Search) is an official place to start looking up information on your property.

If your home was built before 1978, talk to your agent early. They can walk you through the paperwork that applies to your sale. For the exact requirements, use the Tennessee Real Estate Commission and the official federal sources rather than relying on a summary like this one.

I am not going to list every requirement here. The rule is specific, and the current official wording is what counts.

## How disclosures fit with inspections

A disclosure is not an inspection. The disclosure is your statement of what you know. An inspection is a buyer's way of checking the home for themselves.

Termite and wood-destroying organism (WDO) inspections are commonly requested by buyers and lenders in Tennessee. Radon testing, a sewer scope and a termite inspection are also common add-ons to a standard home inspection.

It helps to expect these before you list. The [EPA radon information](https://www.epa.gov/radon) page is a starting point if radon testing is new to you. If you already know about a past termite issue or a repair, your disclosure answers should line up with what you tell your agent.

For some market context, Redfin's rolling three-month data for Franklin, as of October 31, 2026, shows a median of 61 days on market and 4.1 months of supply. Months of supply is how long it would take to sell every active listing at the current pace of sales. On the usual scale, 4 to 6 months is considered balanced.

Those are citywide numbers. Your street, price range and the condition of your home can look different. Local data is useful for planning, but it does not change what you need to disclose. You can see more on the [Market data for the I-65 corridor](/market-data) page.

## Taxes, schools and where you are selling

Buyers often ask about school assignment and property taxes. Both depend on the exact address, so verify them with the school district and the county. Do not rely on a general statement.

That is especially true in Spring Hill, which includes parts of both Williamson and Maury counties. County services, schools and taxes can differ by address there. If you are selling in either area, these pages may help: [Selling a home in Franklin](/franklin/selling-in-franklin) and [Selling a home in Spring Hill](/spring-hill/selling-in-spring-hill).

## A simple way to prepare

Here is a short order of operations:

1. Confirm the year your home was built.
2. Gather repair records, warranties and past reports.
3. Ask your agent which disclosures apply to your sale, and check the Tennessee Real Estate Commission for current forms.

If you want to talk through your situation, start with [Find out what your home is worth](/sell#form). I will go over the disclosures that apply to your home and what to expect from buyers and inspections. There is no pressure to list.

faq.q: What is the Tennessee residential property condition disclosure?
faq.a: Tennessee sellers complete the residential property condition disclosure, or an exemption. It is a written statement of the home's condition, so answer based on what you know and check the Tennessee Real Estate Commission for the current form.

faq.q: Does the lead-based paint disclosure apply to every home?
faq.a: No. The lead-based paint disclosure applies to homes built before 1978. Confirm your home's year built and ask your agent which paperwork applies.

faq.q: Are seller disclosures the same as a home inspection?
faq.a: No. A disclosure is the seller's statement about the home, while an inspection is a check done for the buyer. Termite and WDO inspections are commonly requested by buyers and lenders in Tennessee.

faq.q: What add-on inspections do buyers commonly request?
faq.a: Radon testing, a sewer scope and a termite inspection are common add-ons to a standard home inspection.

faq.q: Do property taxes and schools affect what I disclose?
faq.a: School assignment and property taxes depend on the exact address. Buyers should verify them with the school district and the county.
